summary: MORNING REPORT, 2026-09-17 (written 05:45Z, about 01:45 your time). You asked for a formed basic plan by 9am and for research to finish. Both are done. THE PLAN is the file BUILD_PLAN.md at the top of the pokerbot project on GitHub. Its first page is written for you in plain words: the bot is a search that looks ahead over the game's own rules and finishes each imagined hand with a fixed style; a scoreboard of scripted opponents says whether any change is an improvement before it counts; six stages from a table we trust to sitting at a real table. WHAT LANDED OVERNIGHT, all on the main branch and all tested: (1) the last research document, on pre-computed strategies, so research is closed; (2) the table (T1): the poker engine wrapped for 2 to 9 seats with seven safety checks that abort a run if the table ever misdeals or mispays; (3) the first bot (T2): it played 1,000 hands at a six-seat table against random players with no safety check failing, every decision under a tenth of a second, and won about 2,300 big blinds per 100 hands, which is far above zero even allowing for luck. One honest caveat, written into the project: random players shove so often that nearly every hand ended before the flop, so this score measures the bot's first decision and little else; (4) the scoreboard (T3): four calibration opponents and nine scripted player types with their habits drawn fresh each session, half of them held back so the bot cannot be tuned to them, paired deals, confidence intervals, and a pre-written accept/reject rule weighted 50% six-handed, 30% eight and nine, 20% the rest. It correctly rejects a bot made deliberately worse. Also landed: a one-command test gate for pokerbot, and a manual for Rohit's assistant posted as GitHub issue #13 on the pokerbot repository (send him that link; he had not started as of 05:45Z). ADDED 06:45Z, THE FIRST REAL MEASUREMENT: the first bot was run through the scoreboard against all thirteen scripted opponents at tables of 2, 6, 8 and 9 (500 hands a square, 23 minutes). Verdict ACCEPT: it finished about 2,370 big blinds per 100 hands ahead of a version that calls everything, on the same deals. Of the thirteen it beats seven (the give-up, call-everything, raise-everything and coin-flip players, the one who calls too much, the wild bettor, and the one who plays badly after a big loss), LOSES to two (the player who waits all night for a premium hand, and the tight-aggressive competent player), and is too close to call against four. Honest caveat: these opponents put money in far more freely than people do, so the size of the number says how bad they are, not how good the bot is. The two losses are the next thing to fix, and BUILD_PLAN.md's opponent model is the tool for it. The full report is research/results/stage2_search_vs_personas.txt on GitHub. ADDED 09:10Z: Stage 3 of the plan, the notebook, also landed overnight: it watches every named player, counts their habits, and prints a profile with a confidence beside each number, reproducing the design's worked example exactly. That is the piece the bot will use to play the person rather than the table; Stage 4 wires it into the bot and is the next build. TWO DECISIONS ARE STILL YOURS (queued earlier as report 8983491d91ab): D1 whether to take Rohit's arena and betting-rules fix (recommended yes, once his 24 changes in issue #4 are done), and D2 how the bot will see a real table, which needs you to say where you play. ON THE FLEET SIDE: every session now pushes its own unpushed work when it starts, so you never type a git command again; the sweep can no longer land a change on a stale review or delete a running worker's files; your pace and no-menial-labor decisions are written into the rules; the usage meter that reads your five-hour window and tells the fleet to spread agents evenly across it is in its final review round and lands next.
